# Vessantarajātaka (Ja 547)

**ID:** Ja 547
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Tale of Vessantara

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vessantarajātaka* (Ja 547) is the final and longest narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [Nakanishi 2000; Salomon 2018; Jory 2016]. Set near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Grove, it was told by the Buddha on the occasion of a shower of rain (*pokkharavassa*) [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010; Walker 2022]. The narrative recounts the Bodhisatta's penultimate life as Prince Vessantara, exemplifying the perfection of giving (*dāna*) before his final rebirth as Gotama Buddha [Nakanishi 2000]. Within the Theravāda canon, only the verses (*gāthā*) are considered canonical root text, while the prose framing stems from the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* traditionally ascribed to Buddhaghosa [Jory 2016]. In Southeast Asian traditions, the text is structured into thirteen chapters and is traditionally designated as the *Gāthā Phan* ('Thousand Verses'), although the Pali Text Society edition actually counts 786 verses [Orofino and Vita 2004].

Across Asia, the story circulated widely as a foundational epic of Buddhist ethics and monastic and lay devotion, celebrated in festivals such as Thailand's *Thet Mahachat* or *Bun Phawet* and reflected in fifteenth-century bilingual vernacular renditions like the *Mahāchat Kham Luang* (*Mahājāti gām hlvan*) [Orofino and Vita 2004; Jory 2016; Walker 2022]. Cognate narratives appear in Sanskrit (e.g., Āryaśūra's *Jātakamālā* and the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*), Tibetan (such as *Dri med kun ldan*), Chinese (e.g., in Kang Senghui's *Liuduji jing*, T 152, and T 171/172), Khotanese, Sogdian, and Gāndhārī fragments [Nakanishi 2000; Boucher 2008; Salomon 2018; Williams 2005].

In Pali cross-references, the jātaka is cited in texts such as the *Milindapañha* (Mil 6.3.1, 5.1.4), *Petavatthu* (Pv 21), *Mahāniddesa* (Cnd 22), and *Apadāna* (Tha-Ap 132) [SuttaCentral]. SuttaCentral identifies passage-level parallels in several other Jātakas (Ja 180, Ja 450, Ja 480, Ja 503, Ja 532, Ja 540) and Saṃyutta Nikāya suttas (SN 1.32, SN 1.72) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus registers substantial text reuse with the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Vessantaracariya* (Cp 9), and other late Jātakas including the *Soṇanandajātaka* (Ja 532) and *Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka* (Ja 540), alongside significant cross-language alignments with Tibetan and Sanskrit texts such as the *Jātakamālā*, the *Vinayavastu* / *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and the *Viśvantarāvadāna* [DharmaNexus].
